621.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
621.explanation: In Mahavira's teaching on the twenty-two troubles (parishaha) a monk is to meet illness and misfortune with a cheerful, steady mind instead of distress.
621.tie_back: The Kural's call to smile when trouble comes is matched by the Jain instruction to meet misfortune cheerfully and with a steadied mind.
621.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
621._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A close parallel on cheerful composure under trouble; the Jain context is a monk's illness and ascetic discipline rather than worldly setbacks.

622.quote_or_event: “Is there a shelter, a refuge, a firm ground for the beings carried away by the great flood of water? do you know the island, O Gautama?” … “The flood is old age and death, which carry away living beings; Law is the island, the firm ground, the refuge, the most excellent shelter.”
622.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, the flood that sweeps beings away is answered by the Law (dharma), an island that the flood cannot cover.
622.tie_back: The Kural pictures sorrow as a flood that the wise mind overcomes; the Jain text uses the same flood image and places firm ground against it, though that ground is the Law rather than the mind's own resolve.
622.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 23.65 and 23.68 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
622._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The flood image is shared, but the flood here is old age and death and the refuge is dharma, not a steady mind, so the fit is partial.

623.quote_or_event: “Suffering from insects a great sage remains undisturbed. As an elephant at the head of the battle kills the enemy, so does a hero (in self-control conquer the internal foe).”
623.explanation: Enduring the trouble of biting insects, the sage is compared to a war elephant that turns on and destroys the enemy.
623.tie_back: The Kural says that those who do not grieve at sorrow turn the tables and make sorrow itself suffer; the Jain verse likewise makes the one who endures the attacker who defeats the foe.
623.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
623._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Shares the reversal of attacker and attacked, but the enemy conquered is the inner passions, not the trouble itself, and there is no wordplay like Valluvar's.

624.quote_or_event: “… he was free like a bird; he was always waking like the fabulous bird Bhâruṇḍa, valorous like an elephant, strong like a bull, difficult to attack like a lion, steady and firm like Mount Mandara, deep like the ocean … like the earth he patiently bore everything …”
624.explanation: During his years as a wandering ascetic, the Kalpa Sutra describes Mahavira with a string of similes, among them the strength of a bull and the earth's patience in bearing everything.
624.tie_back: The Kural's image of the ox that pulls the cart through every rut is echoed in the Jain portrait of Mahavira as strong like a bull and bearing everything like the earth.
624.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
624._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (quoted with omissions marked). The bull appears only as one simile in a list; the Kural's picture of hauling through mire is not present, so the match is partial.

625.quote_or_event: “All these troubles have been declared by the Kâśyapa. A monk should not be vanquished by them, when attacked by any anywhere.”
625.explanation: Having listed twenty-two troubles that may strike a monk, often several at once, the lecture closes by saying he must not be overcome by any of them.
625.tie_back: The Kural says that even when troubles come piled on one another, the one who does not break inside defeats them; the Jain conclusion likewise requires the monk to stay undefeated by every trouble, wherever it attacks.
625.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2, closing verse (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
625._accuracy_note: Checked on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi writes 'Kâ*s*yapa' (i.e. Mahavira), normalised here to Kâśyapa. Strong thematic fit; it does not explicitly mention troubles coming in succession.

626.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
626.explanation: When Indra tells King Nami, newly turned monk, that his palace and city are on fire, Nami answers that nothing of his is burning, because he calls nothing his own.
626.tie_back: The Kural asks whether those who never clung to wealth as 'ours' will wail 'we have lost everything'; Nami's reply as Mithila burns is that exact attitude in story form.
626.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
626._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one on non-possessiveness preventing grief at loss; Nami has fully renounced, whereas the Kural speaks of not clinging.

627.quote_or_event: “This body is not permanent, it is impure and of impure origin; it is but a transitory residence (of the soul) and a miserable vessel of suffering.”
627.explanation: Prince Mrigaputra tells his parents why he wants to renounce: the body is impermanent and by its nature a vessel of suffering for the soul (jiva) that dwells in it.
627.tie_back: The Kural says the noble know the body is a target for pain and so are not shaken by it; Mrigaputra likewise sees the body as a natural vessel of suffering.
627.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
627._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on the body as the natural seat of pain; the Jain aim is renunciation of the body, which goes further than the Kural's calm acceptance.

628.quote_or_event: “Not resentful, having few wants, begging from strangers, and not being dainty, a wise man should not long for pleasant things, nor be sorry afterwards (for not having got them).”
628.explanation: Under the trouble of honour and respectful treatment, the monk is told not to crave pleasant things and not to regret their absence.
628.tie_back: The Kural describes one who does not chase pleasure and takes hardship as natural, and so never sinks into misery; the Jain verse prescribes both halves, not longing for pleasant things and not grieving at their lack.
628.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
628._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close in both halves; it does not state the Kural's explicit idea that hardship is natural.

629.quote_or_event: “He was indifferent to success or failure (in begging), to happiness and misery, to life and death, to blame and praise, to honour and insult.”
629.explanation: After renouncing, Mrigaputra is described as unmoved equally by happiness and misery, success and failure.
629.tie_back: The Kural says one who does not revel in good times will not be sunk in bad times; the Jain ideal of equal indifference to happiness and misery is the same balance.
629.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
629._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong parallel of equanimity across pleasure and pain; the Kural's cause-and-effect link (restraint in joy prevents collapse in sorrow) is implied, not stated.

630.quote_or_event: “For more than twelve years the Venerable Ascetic Mahâvira neglected his body and abandoned the care of it; he with equanimity bore, underwent, and suffered all pleasant or unpleasant occurrences arising from divine powers, men, or animals.”
630.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra says Mahavira bore all hardships, from gods, men and animals, with equanimity for more than twelve years before attaining omniscience (kevala), after which gods and men honoured him.
630.tie_back: The Kural promises distinction even enemies admire to one who takes hardship as if it were pleasure; Mahavira's equal acceptance of pleasant and unpleasant ordeals is the Jain model of that, and led to his supreme standing.
630.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §117 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
630._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Good on equanimity in hardship; the Kural's specific reward, admiration even from enemies, is not in this passage and is only implied by Mahavira's later honour.
